extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in the aesthetics of proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Distilling the working aesthetic vocabulary mathematicians use to praise or criticize proofs — i.e., what features make a proof feel 'beautiful' to readers and practitioners. Useful for authors, teachers, and readers assessing proofs' elegance and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof uses few assumptions or previous results and comes together swiftly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued when the argument is direct and relies on minimal prerequisites; simplicity often produces immediate clarity and a sense that the result 'must' be true given the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concision
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof is surprisingly succinct; every part is effective and necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise proofs avoid superfluous steps or detours; terseness should not sacrifice clarity — each component should have a clear role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof derives a result in an unexpected or surprising way, often using an unrelated area of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise can come from a novel connection or technique; unexpectedness increases the aesthetic pleasure by revealing hidden structure or links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof is based on an original or not-before-seen insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original insights (new ideas or approaches) are prized even if the technical content is not long; they change how one thinks about the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof can be easily extended to a larger family of similar problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof that scales or adapts to broader contexts signals conceptual depth and increases perceived value beyond the single result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long, laborious calculations (anti-criterion)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy, tedious computation that lacks conceptual insight is seen as inelegant and detracts from perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy reliance on many previous results (anti-criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy reliance on many previous results -> opaque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a proof depends on a large web of prior theorems, it can feel opaque and reduce the immediacy and elegance of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as an experiential quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty has a strong experiential dimension — felt while working through the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of beauty depends on the process of reading or discovering the proof; the aesthetic impression arises during engagement, not only as an external summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty depends on the audience: "Beauty is in the eye of the beholder."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different audiences (students, specialists, general mathematicians) will value different features; what seems beautiful to one reader may not to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and narrative structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation matters — a beautiful proof should read as a narrative with clear structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposition, ordering of ideas, and clarity of narrative influence perceived beauty; good presentation can make an argument feel natural and inevitable.
